v08_move_to_middle

This experiment tests the visual occlusion effect in mental imagery by using a priming paradigm following Sekuler and Palmer (1992). If subjects are primed by a circle, and then do a same/ different task. they are faster to determine two circles are the same rather than two Pac-Men are the same. If the prime is a Pac-Man, they are faster in the two Pac-Men test. When we see a shape like “Pac-Man” and a square fits perfectly into the missing quarter, our brain fills in the missing part. This makes us perceive the square as if it is overlaid on a complete circle rather than next to a Pac-Man so that it can prime the two circles discrimination task instead of the two Pac-Men condition. We predict this is the same in mental imagery: an imagined partially occluded notched shape is presented as complete. V08 is a control experiment. We ask subjects to imagine moving a corner shape up/down, aligning it with the central shape side by side.

Experiment

https://xh.subjectivityresearch.org/visual_occlusion/v08_move_to_middle/index.html

Stimuli and Task Design

knitr::include_graphics("image/procedure.png")

In this task, each trial begins with a fixation cross appearing in the center of the screen for 250 ms, followed by a 250 ms blank screen. Next, a prime display is shown for 1000 ms, featuring a centered prime shape (either a notched square or a Pac-Man) with an occluder (either a circle or a square) positioned at one of the screen’s four corners. This arrangement results in eight possible types of prime displays. This prime disappears after 1000 ms, leaving an empty screen. Subjects need to imagine the corner shape moving up/down to the middle. Then a test display appears, containing three shapes: an irrelevant shape that mimics the occluder and is positioned further from the center, and a test pair of two shapes in the middle of the screen. The task requires subjects to determine if the test pair shapes are the same or different (key ‘S’ for ‘same’ and key ‘D’ for ‘different’). The same condition includes either two identical shapes (e.g., two circles or two Pac-Men for Pac-Man primes, or two squares or two notched squares for notched square primes), while the different condition includes a pair of different shapes (e.g., a circle and a square or a Pac-Man and a square for Pac-Man primes, or a square and a circle or a notched square and a circle for notched square primes). Feedback is provided based on the response time (RT): if the RT exceeds 1500 ms, a warning message “TOO SLOW! Press the spacebar to continue.” appears, and if the RT is faster than 200 ms, a message “Do not press before the test shapes appear. Press the spacebar to continue.” is displayed. Finally they need to click the button with their mouse to rate the vividness of their mental imagery. 1 = Not vivid at all, 2 = Slightly vivid, 3 = Moderately vivid, 4 = Very vivid, 5 = Extremely vivid. The next trial begins automatically after a 1000 ms delay.

The stimuli box measures 400 pixels, with shapes having a diameter of 67 pixels. In the test display, the irrelevant shape is positioned 58 pixels from the left and 58 pixels from the top, with the test pair shapes spaced 89 pixels apart.

Parameters

  • const itiDuration = 1000; //ms
  • const fixationDuration = 250; //ms
  • const imageDuration = 1000; //ms
  • const imageryDuration = 3000; //ms
  • const maxResponseTime = 1500; //ms
  • const afterFixationInterval = 250; //ms

Subjects

  • Platform: Prolific
  • 14 Aug 2024, 15:48
  • 50 subjects
  • Age: 18–65
  • Current Country of Residence: United Kingdom, United States
  • Normal vision, no Colorblindness, and no mild cognitive impairment/Dementia
  • Approval Rate: 99–100
  • Number of previous submissions: 50–10000
  • ~13 minutes (with instructions and questionnaires)
  • Total study cost: $173.33
  • Study code: C19E4WDH

Key Columns for Analysis

  • Subject: exclude participants with low accuracy (46 left) and outliers (45 left).
  • trialNum: 32 trials per subject.
  • test_shape: complete or notched.
  • prime_shape: circle or square.
  • correct_answer: same or different (only analyze “same”).
  • correct: 0 means incorrect (either slow or press the wrong key); 1 means correct (only analyze “correct”).
  • rt: calculate the mean rt of each condition.

Data preparation

Load the data file

df_input_all <-
  read_csv("v08_move_to_middle_all_subjects_data.csv")
## Rows: 1600 Columns: 17
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr (10): experimentName, subject_id, study_id, session_id, stimulus, respon...
## dbl  (7): subject, rt, prime_type, test_type, correct, trial_num, rating
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

Exclude subjects with low accuracy and outliers

# Function to identify subjects with outliers based on 3SD rule
identify_outliers_3sd <- function(df, column) {
  mean_value <- mean(df[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_value <- sd(df[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
  
  lower_bound <- mean_value - 3 * sd_value
  upper_bound <- mean_value + 3 * sd_value
  
  outliers <- df %>%
    filter(df[[column]] < lower_bound | df[[column]] > upper_bound) %>%
    distinct(subject)  # Get unique subject IDs
  
  return(outliers)
}

# Exclude participants with low accuracy
filtered_subject <- df_input_all %>%
  group_by(subject) %>%
  filter(
    sum(correct == 1 & rt > 200) / n() >= 0.8  
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Only analyze trials with a correct same response
filtered_data <- filtered_subject %>%
  filter(
    correct == 1,
    correct_answer == "same",
    rt > 200
  )

diff_data <- filtered_data %>%
  group_by(subject, prime_shape, test_shape) %>%
  summarise(mean_rt = mean(rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  spread(test_shape, mean_rt) %>%
  mutate(diff = notched - complete) %>%
  select(subject, prime_shape, diff)

# Spread the differences to wide format
diff_wide <- diff_data %>%
  spread(prime_shape, diff)

# Identify outliers for circle and square columns
outliers_circle <- diff_wide %>%
  identify_outliers_3sd("circle")

outliers_square <- diff_wide %>%
  identify_outliers_3sd("square")

# Combine outliers from both columns
outliers_to_exclude <- union(outliers_circle, outliers_square)

# Now do it again
filtered_subject <- df_input_all %>%
  filter(!(subject %in% outliers_to_exclude)) %>%
  group_by(subject) %>%
  filter(
    #subject != 25,
    sum(correct == 1) / n() >= 0.8  
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

Data preparation for RT analysis

# Only analyze trials with a correct same response
filtered_data <- filtered_subject %>%
  filter(
    correct == 1,
    correct_answer == "same",
    rt > 200
  )
# Calculate subjects' average rt and rating for each condition
subject_condition_data_rt <- aggregate(rt ~ subject + prime_shape + test_shape, data = filtered_data, mean)

# Calculate the mean and standard error for rt
mean_data_rt <- aggregate(rt ~ prime_shape + test_shape, data = subject_condition_data_rt, mean)
se_data_rt <- aggregate(rt ~ prime_shape + test_shape, data = subject_condition_data_rt, function(x) sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)))

# Merge the results
plot_data_rt <- merge(mean_data_rt, se_data_rt, by = c("prime_shape", "test_shape"))
colnames(plot_data_rt) <- c("prime_shape", "test_shape", "mean_rt", "se_rt")

# Calculate the Z-score for the 95% confidence interval
z_0.025 <- qnorm(0.975)

# Calculate 95% CI
plot_data_rt$ci_lower <- plot_data_rt$mean_rt - z_0.025 * plot_data_rt$se_rt
plot_data_rt$ci_upper <- plot_data_rt$mean_rt + z_0.025 * plot_data_rt$se_rt

Data analysis

Linear model: compare models

M1 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape * prime_shape + (1 + test_shape + prime_shape | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
M2 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + test_shape + prime_shape | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
anova(M1, M2)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M2: rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + test_shape + prime_shape | subject)
## M1: rt ~ test_shape * prime_shape + (1 + test_shape + prime_shape | subject)
##    npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M2   10 8884.8 8930.1 -4432.4   8864.8                     
## M1   11 8886.8 8936.6 -4432.4   8864.8 0.0294  1     0.8638
## M2 (without interaction) is a better model
## Warning message: boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
## There may be an unnecessary random effect

M3 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + prime_shape | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
M4 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + test_shape | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
anova(M3, M4)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M3: rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + prime_shape | subject)
## M4: rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + test_shape | subject)
##    npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M3    7 8878.9 8910.6 -4432.5   8864.9                    
## M4    7 8879.3 8911.0 -4432.6   8865.3     0  0
## No warning message: prime_shape is the unnecessary random effect.
## M4 is a better model

M5 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
anova(M4, M5)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M5: rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 | subject)
## M4: rt ~ test_shape + prime_shape + (1 + test_shape | subject)
##    npar    AIC  BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M5    5 8875.3 8898 -4432.7   8865.3                     
## M4    7 8879.3 8911 -4432.6   8865.3 0.0234  2     0.9884
## AIC favors M4 while BIC favors M5

### Let's say we use M5 for the following analysis

T test for the difference within each prime condition

# (notched - complete) for square vs. (notched - complete) for circle
# Calculate the differences (notched - complete) within each prime shape
diff_data <- subject_condition_data_rt %>%
  group_by(subject, prime_shape, test_shape) %>%
  summarise(mean_rt = mean(rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  spread(test_shape, mean_rt) %>%
  mutate(diff = notched - complete) %>%
  select(subject, prime_shape, diff)

# Spread the differences to wide format
diff_wide <- diff_data %>%
  spread(prime_shape, diff)

# Perform the paired t-test
t_test_diff <- t.test(diff_wide$square, diff_wide$circle, paired = TRUE)
print(t_test_diff)
## 
##  Paired t-test
## 
## data:  diff_wide$square and diff_wide$circle
## t = -0.44461, df = 44, p-value = 0.6588
## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -49.59103  31.66510
## sample estimates:
## mean difference 
##       -8.962963

Annotations

# Define the function to convert p-values to significance stars
get_significance_stars <- function(p_values) {
  # Apply the case_when logic to each p-value
  stars <- sapply(p_values, function(p_value) {
    case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ "n.s."
    )
  })
  return(stars)
}

p_value_group_difference <- t_test_diff$p.value
p_value_circle_square <- summary_emmeans_M5$p.value
significance_group_difference <- get_significance_stars(p_value_group_difference)
significance_circle_square <- get_significance_stars(p_value_circle_square)

Results of RT analysis

The reaction time for notched shape is significantly longer than the complete, regardless of the prime shape.

Vividness Rating and Imagination Time

Quality check

quality_check <- filtered_subject %>%
  group_by(subject) %>%
  summarise(
    distinct_rating = n_distinct(rating),
    sd_rating = sd(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_rating = max(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_rating = min(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_rating = median(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Create a separate data frame for the max, min, mean, and median
stat_summary <- quality_check %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(max_rating, min_rating, mean_rating, median_rating), 
               names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value")

# Bar plot for the range of ratings with dots
ggplot(quality_check, aes(x = factor(subject), y = distinct_rating)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "gray") +
  geom_point(data = stat_summary, aes(x = factor(subject), y = value, color = statistic), 
             position = position_dodge(width = 0), size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("max_rating" = "red", "min_rating" = "blue", "mean_rating" = "green", "median_rating" = "purple"),
                     labels = c("max_rating" = "Max", "min_rating" = "Min", "mean_rating" = "Mean", "median_rating" = "Median")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +  # Add space at the bottom and top of y-axis
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +  # Add space between bars and left side of plot
  labs(x = "Subject", y = "Ratings", color = "Statistics") +
  theme_classic() +

Rating difference between circle and square

average_ratings <- filtered_subject %>%
  filter(prime_shape %in% c("square", "circle")) %>%
  group_by(subject, prime_shape) %>%
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  spread(prime_shape, mean_rating)

# Perform Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test (in place of the paired t-test)
wilcox_result <- wilcox.test(average_ratings$circle, average_ratings$square, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)
print(wilcox_result)
## 
##  Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  average_ratings$circle and average_ratings$square
## V = 281, p-value = 0.1288
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )

# For Circle
ggplot(data = filtered_data %>% filter(prime_shape == "circle"), aes(x = rating, y = rt, color = test_shape)) +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.3, dodge.width = 0.5, seed = 3922), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +  # Adjust alpha for transparency
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, aes(linetype = test_shape), show.legend = FALSE) +  # Add regression lines
  labs(x = "Rating (Circle)",
       y = "RT (Circle)",
       color = "Test Shape") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(200, 1600, by = 400),
    limits = c(200, 1600)
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )

Ratings and RT (circle/square, and complete/notched separately)

# Plot with different colors and shapes for each condition and adjust position
ggplot(filtered_data, aes(x = rating, y = rt, color = interaction(prime_shape, test_shape), shape = interaction(prime_shape, test_shape))) +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.45, dodge.width = 0.6, seed = 3922), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.5) +  # Adjust alpha for transparency
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, aes(linetype = interaction(prime_shape, test_shape)), show.legend = FALSE) +  # Add regression lines
  labs(x = "Rating",
       y = "RT",
       color = "Condition",
       shape = "Condition") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("circle.complete" = "blue", "circle.notched" = "green", "square.complete" = "red", "square.notched" = "purple")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("circle.complete" = 16, "circle.notched" = 1, "square.complete" = 15, "square.notched" = 0)) +  # Assign different shapes
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("circle.complete" = "solid", "circle.notched" = "dashed", "square.complete" = "solid", "square.notched" = "dashed")) +  # Set linetypes
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(200, 1600, by = 400),
    limits = c(200, 1600)
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )

Ratings and RT (complete and notched separately)

# Collapse across prime_shape, differentiate by test_shape
ggplot(filtered_data, aes(x = rating, y = rt, color = test_shape, shape = test_shape)) +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.3, dodge.width = 0.5, seed = 3922), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +  # Adjust alpha for transparency
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, aes(linetype = test_shape), show.legend = FALSE) +  # Add regression lines
  labs(x = "Rating",
       y = "RT",
       color = "Test Shape",
       shape = "Test Shape") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("complete" = 16, "notched" = 1)) +  # Assign different shapes
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("complete" = "solid", "notched" = "dashed")) +  # Set linetypes
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(200, 1600, by = 400),
    limits = c(200, 1600)
  ) +

  )

### Spearman correlation

# Spearman correlation for complete test_shape
spearman_complete <- cor.test(filtered_data$rating[filtered_data$test_shape == "complete"],
                              filtered_data$rt[filtered_data$test_shape == "complete"],
                              method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

# Spearman correlation for notched test_shape
spearman_notched <- cor.test(filtered_data$rating[filtered_data$test_shape == "notched"],
                             filtered_data$rt[filtered_data$test_shape == "notched"],
                             method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

print(spearman_complete)
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  filtered_data$rating[filtered_data$test_shape == "complete"] and filtered_data$rt[filtered_data$test_shape == "complete"]
## S = 7317418, p-value = 0.07152
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##         rho 
## -0.09757582
print(spearman_notched)
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  filtered_data$rating[filtered_data$test_shape == "notched"] and filtered_data$rt[filtered_data$test_shape == "notched"]
## S = 6898107, p-value = 0.7571
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##         rho 
## -0.01673915

Linear model: compare models

# here the rating is converted to different categories rather than continuous numbers
filtered_data$rating <- as.factor(filtered_data$rating)

M6 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape * rating + (1 + test_shape + rating | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
M7 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + test_shape + rating | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
## Warning: Model failed to converge with 1 negative eigenvalue: -1.9e+01
anova(M6, M7)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M7: rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + test_shape + rating | subject)
## M6: rt ~ test_shape * rating + (1 + test_shape + rating | subject)
##    npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M7   28 8920.7 9047.5 -4432.3   8864.7                     
## M6   32 8923.5 9068.5 -4429.7   8859.5 5.1722  4     0.2701
## M7 (without interaction) is a better model
## Warning message: boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
## There may be an unnecessary random effect

M8 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + rating | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
M9 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + test_shape | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
anova(M8, M9)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M9: rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + test_shape | subject)
## M8: rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + rating | subject)
##    npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M9   10 8889.7 8935.0 -4434.8   8869.7                     
## M8   22 8909.8 9009.5 -4432.9   8865.8 3.8898 12     0.9853
## M9 is a better model

M10 <- lmer(rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 | subject), REML = F, data = filtered_data)
anova(M9, M10)
## Data: filtered_data
## Models:
## M10: rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 | subject)
## M9: rt ~ test_shape + rating + (1 + test_shape | subject)
##     npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## M10    8 8885.7 8921.9 -4434.8   8869.7                     
## M9    10 8889.7 8935.0 -4434.8   8869.7 0.0276  2     0.9863
## AIC favors M9 while BIC favors M10
